keyVerseText: Of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars; the company of the Ashurites have made thy benches of ivory, brought out of the isles of Chittim. the company: or, they have made thy hatches of ivory well trodden company: Heb. daughter
rootMeaning: The root of מָשׁוֹט (mâshôwṭ) is שׁוּט (shûwṭ), which primarily means to go or move about, often with the sense of pushing forth or traveling to and fro. This root imagery enriches the noun מָשׁוֹט beyond the simple English term "oar" by emphasizing the active motion and guidance involved in rowing or navigating. Thus, an oar is not merely a tool but an instrument of purposeful movement and direction on the water.
usageInScripture: The word מָשׁוֹט appears only twice in Scripture, consistently translated as "oar" or "thine oars," indicating a very specific and literal use. Its limited occurrences focus on the practical aspect of navigation, particularly in the context of ships, as seen in the plural form מִשּׁוֹטַיִךְ in Ezekiel 27:6. This consistent translation underscores the tangible, physical role of the oar in steering and propelling vessels, highlighting its importance in ancient maritime culture.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מָשׁוֹט as an oar rooted in the concept of purposeful movement invites reflection on God's guidance and providence in the believer's journey. Just as an oar directs a ship through uncertain waters, so God's Word and Spirit guide the Christian through life's challenges. This word reminds us of the active role believers must take in rowing in faith, cooperating with divine direction. It also points to the Creator's sovereignty over creation, including the seas and navigation, affirming His control over all circumstances.
keyVerseReflection: Ezekiel 27:6 states, "Of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars; the company of the Ashurites have made thy benches of ivory." Here, מָשׁוֹט highlights the craftsmanship and strength of the ship's oars, made from sturdy oaks, symbolizing power and stability. The mention of the oars emphasizes the ship's readiness and ability to navigate, which metaphorically reflects the necessity of reliable tools for moving forward, both physically and spiritually.
